title: Question 11
stem:
The circuit for a full-wave rectifier using four ideal diodes is shown in Fig. 11.1.

{{figure:figure_11_1}}

Fig. 11.1

A resistor $R$ is connected across the output $AB$ of the rectifier.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: draw a circle around any diodes that conduct when the terminal $X$ of the input is positive with respect to terminal $Y$,

markscheme_points.text: circles drawn only around the top left and bottom right diodes

hints: Hint 1: Start at the positive input X and remember current can only flow forward through a diode in the direction of its arrow - trace which two diagonal paths can make a complete loop through R back to Y.
parts.proper_answer: Circle the top-left diode and the bottom-right diode only.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow the current from the positive terminal**
Think of X as pushing current out when it is positive with respect to Y. From the top junction the current must find a forward-pointing diode to leave, go through the load R, and then find a second forward-pointing diode to return to Y at the bottom junction.

Step 2: **Identify the conducting pair**
Only the diode on the top-left side (top to left) and the diode on the bottom-right side (right to bottom) point in the correct sense to allow the loop $$X \rightarrow \text{left} \rightarrow B \rightarrow R \rightarrow A \rightarrow \text{right} \rightarrow Y$$. The other two diodes are reverse-biased and block.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: label the positive (+) and the negative (-) terminals of the output $AB$.

markscheme_points.text: B shown as (+)ve and A shown as (–)ve

hints: Hint 1: Use the conducting diodes you found in (i) to see which way current flows through resistor R - current always flows from higher to lower potential outside the source.
parts.proper_answer: Terminal B is positive (+) and terminal A is negative (-).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the direction through R**
With the top-left and bottom-right diodes conducting, current arrives at the left junction and travels via the lower wire to B, then up through R to A, then back to Y. So through R the flow is from B toward A.

Step 2: **Assign + and -**
Since conventional current flows from positive to negative through a resistor, the end where it enters must be positive. That makes $$B \text{ positive (+), } A \text{ negative (-)}$$ for this half-cycle. In full-wave action this polarity stays the same every half-cycle.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The variation with time $t$ of the potential difference $V$ across the input $XY$ is given by the expression

$$V = 5.6\sin380t$$

where $V$ is measured in volts and $t$ is measured in seconds.

The variation with time $t$ of the rectified potential difference across the resistor $R$ is shown in Fig. 11.2.

{{figure:figure_11_2}}

Fig. 11.2

Use the expression for the input potential difference $V$, or otherwise, to determine
parts.text: the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) potential difference $V_{\text{r.m.s.}}$ of the input,
hints: Hint 1: Look at the form $V = V_0 \sin \omega t$ and pick out what $5.6$ represents for a sine wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link peak to r.m.s.**
For a sine wave the peak value $V_0$ and the root-mean-square value are linked because r.m.s. gives the equivalent d.c. heating effect. You know $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Step 2: **Insert the peak**
Here $$V_0 = 5.6\text{ V}$$ so $$V_{r.m.s.} = \frac{5.6}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 4.0\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the number of times per second that the rectified potential difference at the output reaches a peak value.
hints: Hint 1: Compare $V = 5.6 \sin 380t$ with the standard $V = V_0 \sin \omega t$ to identify the angular frequency and recall how $\omega$ links to ordinary frequency $f$.
Hint 2: Think about what Fig. 11.2 shows - both the positive and negative halves of the input become positive peaks, so how many output peaks occur for each input cycle?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the input frequency**
The sine argument gives angular frequency $$\omega = 380\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ Since $$\omega = 2\pi f$$ then $$f = \frac{380}{2\pi} \approx 60.5\text{ Hz}$$ This is the number of full input cycles per second.

Step 2: **Double for full-wave rectification**
A bridge rectifier inverts the negative half-cycle, so you get two output peaks per input cycle. Hence $$\text{peaks per second} = 2f \approx 121 \approx 120$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: A capacitor is now connected between the terminals $AB$ of the output. The capacitor reduces the variation (the ripple) in the output to $1.6\text{ V}$.
parts.text: On Fig. 11.2, sketch the variation with time $t$ of the smoothed output voltage for time $t = t_1$ to time $t = t_2$.

markscheme_points.text: three lines from near peak showing concave curves after lea not 'kinked' and not cutting the peak reaching candidate's minimum at the point where the decay
three lines drawn along the dotted lines showing rise in volta

hints: Hint 1: Recall that a smoothing capacitor charges to the peak of the rectified wave but then holds the voltage up when the supply falls - what does this say about the peak level?
Hint 2: The ripple is given as 1.6 V, so starting from the ~5.6 V peak, how far down should each trough go?
Hint 3: Picture the discharge between peaks as a gradual exponential fall through the resistor, not a sharp V-shape.
Hint 4: Picture what happens when the next rectified peak rises to meet the falling curve - the voltage must then jump up steeply along the original dotted curve.
parts.proper_answer: Sketch from $t_1$ to $t_2$ with same peaks at ~5.6 V, troughs at ~4.0 V (5.6 - 1.6), smooth concave exponential falls from near each peak, then steep rises along the dotted rectified curve; three such ripples between $t_1$ and $t_2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep the peaks the same**
The capacitor charges up to the full rectified peak, so the tops of your smoothed wave just touch the dotted peaks at about $$5.6\text{ V}$$. The capacitor cannot increase the peak.

Step 2: **Set the ripple depth**
Ripple $= V_{max} - V_{min} = 1.6\text{ V}$. So $$V_{min} \approx 5.6 - 1.6 = 4.0\text{ V}$$ All minima between $t_1$ and $t_2$ sit on the $4.0\text{ V}$ line, well above zero.

Step 3: **Draw the slow discharge**
Between peaks the diodes block and the capacitor discharges through R. Draw three smooth, concave decay curves starting from just after each peak and falling to $4.0\text{ V}$. They must not be kinked and must not cut through the dotted peak.

Step 4: **Draw the fast recharge**
When the next incoming rectified hump catches up, the diodes conduct again and the capacitor recharges rapidly. Draw three short steep rises that follow the dotted sine curve back up to the next peak.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect, if any, on the mean power dissipation in resistor $R$ when the capacitor is connected between terminals $AB$.

markscheme_points.text: mean p.d. is higher or r.m.s. p.d. is higher or capacitor supplies energy to resistor

hints: Hint 1: Compare the average level of the smoothed wave in (c)(i) with the unsmoothed wave that falls to zero - which has the larger mean or r.m.s. voltage?
Hint 2: Recall how power in a resistor depends on voltage, $P = V^2/R$ for mean values, to decide what a higher mean voltage does to heating.
parts.proper_answer: Mean power increases because smoothing raises the mean (and r.m.s.) p.d. across R; the capacitor stores charge at the peak and supplies energy to R during discharge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See the voltage is held up**
Without the capacitor the output falls to zero twice per cycle. With the capacitor it only falls to $4.0\text{ V}$, so both the mean p.d. and the r.m.s. p.d. are larger. Physically the capacitor discharges through R, supplying extra energy between peaks.

Step 2: **Link to power**
Mean power is $$P_{mean} = \frac{V_{r.m.s.}^2}{R}$$ A larger $V_{r.m.s.}$ with the same $R$ means greater mean power dissipation and more heating in R.
